themes.title: Agent verification is trajectory- and evidence-centric
themes.summary: Prefix Executability checks intermediate tool-call validity; VeriCUA gathers evidence; EnvOS tests response to mid-task changes and grader soundness. This is a shared evaluation focus, not one common architecture.

themes.title: Multi-agent reasoning meets serving systems
themes.summary: EpiAgent studies beliefs about other agents for action planning; MAServeBench models collaboration-generated workloads for serving hardware.

themes.title: Embodied work spans simulation scale and model fidelity
themes.summary: Gym-Anything uses coding agents to build and audit robot simulations; world2vec learns latent dynamics intended to capture system behavior more faithfully.

themes.title: Resource constraints are explicit experimental variables
themes.summary: The looped-transformer study tests model size, training compute, and decoding; TextSeal2 evaluates watermark detection under speculative decoding; Rethinking Pre-pretraining compares compute-matched training choices.

open_problems.title: Executable prefixes under partial observability
open_problems.problem: Prefix Executability assumes explicit schemas, preconditions, and benchmark-visible state, and does not certify semantic correctness or safety.
open_problems.direction: Test learned state estimation, matched schema-constrained decoding and repair controls, repeated seeds, and additional domains.

open_problems.title: Verifier cost and missing evidence
open_problems.problem: VeriCUA reports high tool/model-call cost and abstention when recordings do not contain the needed evidence.
open_problems.direction: Measure accuracy–coverage–cost curves under fixed budgets and test lightweight instrumentation that reduces abstention without creating false confidence.

open_problems.title: Simulation breadth and real-world transfer
open_problems.problem: Gym-Anything identifies broader physical-work coverage as future work; the current evaluation is simulated.
open_problems.direction: Expand held-out material/task families and test policies on corresponding real tasks to measure transfer from audited simulation.

open_problems.title: Dynamic environment robustness
open_problems.problem: EnvOS focuses on stale information, results vary by model and interface, and one reported insurance result is not significant after multiple-test correction.
open_problems.direction: Run larger balanced studies varying change type, timing, notice, and interface with preregistered correction-aware comparisons.

open_problems.kind: synthesized direction tied to reported setup
open_problems.title: Strategic generalization
open_problems.problem: EpiAgent reports gains in mixed and competitive scenarios, but the abstract does not establish transfer to unseen opponents or information structures.
open_problems.direction: Test held-out game rules and opponent populations, measuring belief calibration as well as task reward.

sections.title: Prefix Executability: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success
sections.abstract: Proposes trajectory-level metrics for whether tool-call prefixes remain executable, and finds that final-success rankings can hide invalid intermediate execution while plan checking can improve prefix reliability.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The manuscript identifies NeurIPS 2026, Datasets and Benchmarks Track; a matching NeurIPS poster and an independent technical explainer are checkable external signals. Its two-category placement and three-benchmark audit strengthen its relevance to agent evaluation.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce Prefix Executability Curves, First-Error Depth, Trajectory Executability Rate, AUC-PEC, and Recovery Rate to evaluate trajectory validity beyond terminal success.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors describe this as an audit, not a complete leaderboard: BFCL-v3 and ToolSandbox each use 200 sampled tasks, and tau-cubed coverage is limited to Airline/Retail base splits. The metrics assume explicit schemas and benchmark-visible state and do not certify semantic correctness, safety, privacy, or fairness.

sections.title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
sections.abstract: Introduces a platform-agnostic computer-use-agent verifier that actively gathers GUI or code evidence and reports improved agreement with reference labels across offline and online evaluations.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Cross-listed across three core AI categories; the paper reports offline and online tests across platforms, and an independent arXiv TL;DR page also summarizes the work. Ranked for this breadth and concrete evaluation evidence, not for presumed readership.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors use rubric-guided exploration and explicit evidence rules to verify tasks from retained trajectories or accessible post-execution state.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors report that verification can require tens of tool and model calls per trajectory—about an order of magnitude more than a one-call judge. Offline verification abstains when recordings lack evidence, while online access helps only in instrumentable environments.

sections.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
sections.abstract: Presents a framework in which coding agents build and audit realistic robot simulations, yielding RoboWorld and several learning approaches that improve performance on its tasks.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Cross-listed across robotics, AI, and machine learning; the paper reports 25 simulations and 200 train/test environments, and a public project site provides the benchmark and code. The category breadth and reproducible artifact are the main placement signals.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors automate simulation creation through a coding-agent creation/audit loop and report that privileged-state teaching, repeated attempts, and generated demonstrations improve simulated-task performance.
sections.unique_caveat: The evidence is on the paper's 25-simulation RoboWorld suite; real-world transfer is a motivation, not established by these experiments. The paper also says its current coverage should be broadened.

sections.title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
sections.abstract: Presents a watermark designed to retain detection under speculative decoding without changing the target-model output distribution, with improved detection over two comparators in the reported tests.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Three-category cross-listing spans AI, language, and security; the abstract gives controlled comparisons at matched diversity and speculative-decoding acceptance rates, evaluated on three LLMs.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors combine watermark keys through a Gaussian-copula construction and use memoryless exponential races to preserve the watermark through speculative decoding.
sections.unique_caveat: The reported evaluation uses three LLMs; the abstract does not establish that the same detection gains hold across a broader range of models and deployment settings.

sections.title: EpiAgent: Epistemic Self-Play for LLM Agents
sections.abstract: Proposes LLM agents with a learnable belief layer and alternating self-play optimization, reporting gains over prompting and reinforcement-learning baselines in mixed and competitive scenarios.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: It is cross-listed in three core categories, including multi-agent systems, and reports comparisons across both mixed and competitive interactions plus analyses of belief accuracy and action planning.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors separate belief updating from action planning and jointly optimize them through epistemic self-play using prediction of later observations as an intrinsic reward.
sections.unique_caveat: The abstract's empirical claims concern the paper's mixed and competitive scenarios; broad transfer to other strategic settings or opponent populations is not established there.

sections.title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning
sections.abstract: Introduces reward-free latent-dynamics learning intended to make world models more faithful and interpretable, reporting continuous pixel-control results and system identification over 71 attractors with fewer parameters than three named baselines.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The abstract reports a 71-attractor system-identification benchmark and comparisons with DreamerV3, TD-MPC2, and LeWM, including a claimed order-of-magnitude parameter reduction; this is a technically concrete signal despite single-category placement.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors train a mechanistic latent dynamics model directly from observations and actions without reward information.
sections.unique_caveat: Reported evidence focuses on continuous pixel-control environments and the 71-attractor benchmark; generality beyond these task families is not established by the abstract.

sections.title: EnvOS: Auditing Computer-Use Agents When the World Moves On : Phenomenon-Based Task Construction, Certification, and Evidence-Based Evaluation
sections.abstract: Introduces a framework for generating and certifying software environments that change during agent tasks, and evaluates how agents respond to stale information while auditing the graders themselves.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The authors test environment changes, task solvability, and grader quality, reporting controlled clinic-booking and insurance scenarios and a separate corrupted-episode audit. The paper supplies a distinct stress test for computer-use-agent evaluation.
sections.claimed_contribution: EnvOS certifies mid-task changes before execution and independently rechecks episode verdicts against archived evidence.
sections.unique_caveat: The abstract focuses on stale-information changes. It reports that the insurance-claim improvement for one model was not significant after correcting for all tests, so those results are scenario- and model-dependent.

sections.title: How to Loop Your Transformer: Loop Scaling, Specialization, and Parallel Inference
sections.abstract: Studies weight sharing through repeated transformer loops across models up to 1B parameters and 155B training tokens, finding that benefits depend on compute constraints and that looping can slow decoding unless parallel designs preserve quality.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The paper covers two core categories and provides broad scale comparisons—up to 1B parameters, 155B tokens, and 32 loops—across model-size, training-compute, and inference constraints.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors compare loop placement and information flow, test loop-specific low-rank adapters, and propose a parallel-loop design whose quality improves when current-token and previous-token states are normalized separately.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors report that added loops can saturate, reverse, or become unstable; their original parallel formulation does not consistently retain ordinary-loop quality gains.

sections.title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
sections.abstract: Introduces a benchmark that models collaboration patterns as configurable multi-agent serving workloads and links realized operations to latency and hardware behavior.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: This is a focused contribution in the configured multi-agent category. Its composable workload stages and hierarchical traces target a concrete gap between isolated request benchmarks and dependent agent workflows; the abstract links the benchmark to GPU/NPU measurements and reproducible comparisons.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors make collaboration structure a configurable benchmark dimension and connect task completion measurements to serving execution and hardware behavior.
sections.unique_caveat: The benchmark is built around documented multi-agent workflows; conclusions about workloads outside those configurations require further coverage.

sections.title: Rethinking Pre-pretraining
sections.abstract: Reports that four synthetic pre-pretraining curricula do not beat compute-matched natural-language training across three tested regimes, while some gains under extra compute persist only at small natural-language budgets.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The authors test four synthetic curricula under three compute/data regimes and probe initialization sensitivity, forgetting, and interleaving; this broad controlled comparison makes it a useful counterpoint to positive synthetic-data claims.
sections.claimed_contribution: The paper argues that synthetic pre-pretraining as a distinct compute-sharing stage has limited benefit in its matched experiments and examines how initialization and later natural-language training affect reported gains.
sections.unique_caveat: The result is bounded by the four curricula and model/training regimes studied; the paper itself reports residual gains when extra compute is allocated at small natural-language budgets.
